I fixed the accent bug using only the standard library, and I did not add a dependency or the per-locale rules system. `python3 -m unittest` passes, including a new test for "Crème Brûlée" and "Straße Ørsted".

**Change:** `slugify` in `text.py` now decomposes accented letters with `unicodedata.normalize("NFKD")` and drops the combining marks, so "Crème Brûlée" becomes `creme-brulee`. A small table handles letters that don't decompose: ß, æ, œ, ø, ł, đ.

**Why no library or locale system:**
- **Dependency:** the bug only affects Latin-script accents. For those, the standard library gives the same result as python-slugify or Unidecode. A new dependency would only pay off for non-Latin scripts such as Cyrillic, Greek, CJK or Arabic. Nothing in the repo suggests the recipe blog needs those.
- **Locale rules:** a pluggable per-locale system has no second language to design against. It would likely be built wrong and then need rework. Post URLs also come from `slugify(title)` with no locale argument, so `Post` has no locale to pass in.
- **Slug stability:** changing the slug rules later changes already-published URLs, so the rules are worth getting right once.

**Decision for you:** if you do expect non-Latin titles, or a locale-specific rule such as German ä→ae, say which languages. I'll then add Unidecode or python-slugify and a locale hook shaped around those cases. I'd also add a `locale` field to `Post` at that point.

**Existing URLs:** any already-published post whose title contained an accent now gets a different URL. Add redirects if those URLs are live.

`dedupe_events` is quadratic because `seen_list` is a `list` (events.py:22, 25).

`e["id"] not in seen_list` scans the list linearly, comparing against every id seen so far. Each unique id adds one element, so the scan gets longer as the loop goes. With n events and u unique ids, the cost is roughly O(n·u). When most ids are unique, that is O(n²).

For about 200k events that is on the order of 10¹⁰ string comparisons in the worst case, which is why it takes minutes. The `append` calls and the loop itself are cheap by comparison.

The fix is to track seen ids in a `set`, which makes each membership check O(1) on average and the whole function O(n). Keep the `unique` list for output so first-occurrence order is preserved. I haven't changed anything.

I fixed the accent bug with the standard library only. I did not add a transliteration dependency or the per-locale rules system. Tests pass, including a new one for `"Crème Brûlée"` → `"creme-brulee"`.

**What changed:** `slugify` in `text.py` now decomposes the string with `unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", ...)` and drops the combining marks before the existing regex runs. `test_text.py` has the new accent test.

**Why I skipped the locale system:** nothing in the repo needs it yet. `slugify` has one caller (`Post.url`) and no locale field. A plugin API designed before there's a real case would probably be the wrong shape.

**Where the stdlib approach stops:**
- It can't transliterate characters that aren't base letter plus accent: `ß`, `æ`, `ø`, `đ`, and Cyrillic, Greek, CJK.

**Risk:** any already-published post whose title has accents now gets a different URL. Before the fix, `Crème` came out as `cr-me`. If those URLs are public or indexed, you need redirects or stored slugs.

**Cause:** `migrate.py` re-ran every `.sql` file on each run and kept no record of what had already been applied. `app.db` already had the `email` column from `002_add_email.sql`, so that migration's `ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMN` failed.

**Other databases:** any other copy of the database that already has `email` but no `schema_migrations` table will hit the same error. It needs the same one-time marking of `001` and `002`.
